assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/3jLd4kNqR7mZpW2vXcT8b1
assertions.basis: Standard sira/maghazi tradition: Ali carried the Muhajirun banner and, per widely repeated accounts, personally accounted for several of the enemy's standard-bearers. Not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/4tVbN6yHjM3kQ9wErZ7uXs1
assertions.basis: Hamza b. Abd al-Muttalib led the counter-charge alongside Ali per the standard tradition. Not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/7yUmK3jHgF9dSaQ2wErT5z1
assertions.basis: Sa'd b. Mu'adh, chief of Aws, led the Ansar battalion at Badr per the standard tradition.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/4sDfG6hJkQ2wErT9yUmNbV1
assertions.basis: Ubaydah b. al-Harith fought in the pre-battle triple duel (with Hamza and Ali) against three Qurashi champions; he was mortally wounded (his leg severed) and died of the wound shortly afterward, on the return march. Widely repeated in the standard sira tradition, not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/8gY3kPcU5nR8yAdW3jS9eE1
assertions.basis: Uthman b. Affan stayed in Madinah to nurse his ill wife Ruqayyah bint Muhammad, who died during the Badr campaign; the Prophet allotted him a share of the spoils as though he had been present. Standard sira tradition.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/9kQwE7rTyU4mNbV6cXzAsD1
assertions.basis: Talha b. Ubaydullah was sent with Sa'id b. Zayd to Syria to gather intelligence on the Meccan caravan and returned after the battle; both were given shares of the spoils as though present. Standard sira tradition.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/5zAsD3fGhJ7kQwE4rTyUmN1
assertions.basis: Sa'id b. Zayd was on the same Syria intelligence mission as Talha b. Ubaydullah (see above).

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/3wY6xZc2mQ7vR9nK4pT8sA1
assertions.basis: Ja'far b. Abi Talib was in Abyssinia with the second group of migrants at the time of Badr; he returned to Madinah only around the time of Khaybar (7 AH). Standard sira tradition.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/2mQ7vR9nK4pT8sY3wZ6xCe
assertions.subjectLabel: The Prophet Muḥammad (peace and blessings be upon him)
assertions.basis: Seed dataset item 031 (Cave of Thawr): The Prophet (peace be upon him) and Abu Bakr remained concealed in Ghar Thawr during the Hijra (cf. the fuller worked example in ontology/examples/thawr.ttl, a separate, independently-identified encoding of the same tradition -- reconciling the two identities is scholar review work, not pre-empted here). No source edition attached yet -- pending scholarly citation.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/9kQwE7rTyU4mNbV6cXzAsD1
assertions.basis: Talha b. Ubaydullah shielded the Prophet at Uhud, sustaining multiple wounds and reportedly losing the use of a hand — remembered as 'Talha of the day of Uhud'. Standard tradition; not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/9qWeR4tYuP7aSdF3gHjKzX1
assertions.basis: Sa'd b. Abi Waqqas fought as an archer at Uhud; widely-repeated tradition has the Prophet urging him on with 'shoot, may my father and mother be sacrificed for you'. Not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/3jLd4kNqR7mZpW2vXcT8b1
assertions.basis: Ali fought and killed the Qurashi champion Amr b. Abd Wudd in single combat when he crossed the trench; no other warrior crossed again afterward. Standard tradition; not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/8gY3kPcU5nR8yAdW3jS9eE1
assertions.objectLabel: Ḥudaybiyya and the Pledge of Riḍwān
assertions.basis: Uthman was sent by the Prophet as an envoy to the Quraysh in Makkah during this expedition; his delay caused rumour of his death, prompting the Pledge itself. The Prophet reportedly struck his own hand as a pledge made on Uthman's behalf. He was present at the wider expedition but absent from the pledge under the tree. Standard tradition; not yet matched to a specific passage.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/3wY6xZc2mQ7vR9nK4pT8sA1
assertions.objectLabel: Ḥudaybiyya and the Pledge of Riḍwān
assertions.basis: Ja'far b. Abi Talib was still in Abyssinia at this date, returning only around the time of Khaybar (7 AH) — after Hudaybiyya. See his Badr-absence assertion for the same underlying fact.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/2aSdF6gHjK8mNbV5cXzQwE1
assertions.basis: Bilal is reported to have given the call to prayer from the roof of the Kaaba at the conquest — found in early sources including Musannaf Ibn Abi Shayba and the works of Ibn Hisham and al-Bayhaqi, but ⟨scholar⟩ this specific detail is NOT established via an authenticated connected narration in Sahih al-Bukhari or Sahih Muslim, despite being widely repeated. Rendered here at reduced confidence deliberately — a real example of the gap between 'widely repeated' and 'authenticated'.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/event/6xZc2mQ7vR9nK4pT8sY3wA3
assertions.basis: Widely dated to 12 Rabi al-Awwal, 11 AH (8 June 632 CE); the exact day is itself a point of scholarly disagreement (some accounts favour the 1st or 2nd of the month) — see the Dispute object for this Event.

assertions.subject: https://w3id.org/marsad/id/person/8sT3wY6xZc2mQ7vR9nK4pP1
assertions.basis: Abu Bakr led the congregational prayers during the Prophet's final illness, at his instruction — a well-attested tradition, historically cited by some as bearing on the succession, a question this file does not adjudicate.

coverageGap.description: The Companions are estimated at well over 100,000 (Abu Zur'ah al-Razi, via al-Suyuti). This file represents ~35 of them: a curated, historically prominent, documentable set, chosen to demonstrate the network's true shape rather than to claim any completeness. The Badr and Uhud participant lists are similarly highlight sets, not rosters — real Badr had ~313 Muslims present, and Uhud a comparable order of magnitude. Second-generation (Tabi'un) individuals are entirely out of scope for this file by design, per project direction — see docs/09 roadmap. The events between Uhud (3 AH) and the Prophet's death (11 AH) are represented by five milestones (Uhud, Khandaq, Hudaybiyya, the Conquest of Makkah, the Prophet's death) chosen for documentability, not as a complete chronicle — many attested events in this span (Khaybar, the expedition to Tabuk, the Farewell Pilgrimage, among others) are not yet modelled.

This file adds ~100 incidents spanning the full Prophetic era and the Rashidun succession, compiled directly by the project maintainer as seed material rather than through independent AI research (see file header). It is not scholar-reviewed, not matched to specific source passages or editions, and its approximate CE datings are conventional, not calendar-precise. Several named groups mentioned in the source incidents (the Ansar as a body, the Quraysh delegation to Abyssinia, the confederate tribes at the Trench) are referenced only generically and are not individually modelled. This is exactly the material the step-by-step roadmap ('The Road Ahead') describes as needing a real review workbench and real historians before any of it can be marked verified.
